newsitem.title: GUAM: S.Korean jumbo jet crashes in Guam, 35 survive.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean jumbo jet crashes in Guam, 35 survive.

text.p: More than 200 people died when a South Korean jumbo jet crashed on this U.S. Pacific island early on Wednesday, but 35 survived including some who walked away from burning wreckage, officials and witnesses said.

The Korean Air Lines Boeing 747 flying mostly South Korean tourists and honeymooners from Seoul crashed in heavy rain and ruptured an oil pipeline just miles from the airport and not far from the island's most heavily populated area.

Andrew Murphy, spokesman for the Guam Airport Authority, said the number of survivors taken to hospital had risen to 35. He declined to comment on a Korean Air Lines official's statement that at least 55 people out of 254 passengers and crew may have survived.

Hours after the airliner crashed and burst into flames on a hillside, rescue workers searched frantically for more survivors, widening the search area to look for people who may have been flung out by the impact.
"We are continuing to go to the wreckage site to make sure that there is no one we are not able to find," a spokeswoman for Guam Governor Carl Gutierrez said.
Eyewitnesses said the crash impact split the aircraft into five parts and it was miraculous that some people managed to escape.

"I saw some people were able to walk away from the wreckage. The plane was in five pieces and it's a miracle that anyone could come out of this," said Dr Michael Lancer, a Guam resident who reached the wreckage while it was still burning.

Officials in Seoul said Korean Air Lines Flight 801 was carrying 231 passengers and 23 crew, including dozens of vacationers, several South Korean politicians, three infants and at least 14 Americans.
After the night-time crash, rescuers used floodlights to illuminate the site, located in rough terrain in a sparsely populated area called Nimitz.
As dawn broke over the Pacific island territory, what appeared to be a wing and other fragments of wreckage were silhouetted against the trees on the hillside.
Rescuers said the grass in the area, up to five feet (1.7 metres) tall, and the rains at night made movement extremely difficult.
Rear Admiral Martin Janzack, the top U.S. Navy official in Guam, said the two flight recorders had been found and sent to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) in Honolulu, Hawaii.
Governor Gutierrez, one of the first people to reach the crash scene, said he saved five people, including a Korean mother and daughter who "wouldn't let go of each other".
He added: "They were embedded into the steel and the cushions." Eventually, a doctor "yanked" the girl out and the mother followed her, he said.
Gutierrez also pulled out an 11-year-old Japanese girl but flames stopped him from going back into the wreckage to save her mother. "The mother was dead in the flames," Gutierrez said.

Gutierrez said he was told by survivor Barry Small of New Zealand, a helicopter pilot and mechanic who was sitting in row 13 of the plane, that there were no indications of trouble in mid-flight or during the approach to the landing.
Gutierrez said the crash scene was pitch black and rescuers had to follow the screams of survivors.

"The fire (from the plane) was not so big, so we had to follow the sounds. It was eerie and as we got closer I heard all the screams coming from the dark spots ... We had to follow the sounds," he said.

Gutierrez said one woman walked away unscathed from the crash save for a few scratches. Guam Memorial Hospital doctor Edwardo Cruz said the woman was a stewardess who said the plane started to shake just before the crash. The shaking was followed by a big bang, he quoted her as saying.
Airline officials said Shin Ki-ha, a former South Korean parliamentary leader of the opposition National Congress for New Politics, his wife and 20 party members were on the plane.
The U.S. National Transportation Safety Board has started a probe into the cause of the crash, chairman Jim Hall said.
He told a Seattle news conference that investigators would be looking into why a vital piece of airport safety equipment was not in service for the landing.
Air safety sources said visibility at the time was limited to about one mile (1.6 km) due to the heavy rain.
An FAA spokeswoman said the plane had just been cleared for landing at 2:35 a.m. local time on Wednesday (12:35 p.m. EDT on Tuesday) (1635 GMT on Tuesday) when radar contact was lost.
The crash came little more than a year after a TWA Boeing 747 exploded in mid-air off New York, killing 230 people.
Guam, largest of the Mariana Islands in the Western Pacific, is an unincorporated territory of the United States with a population of about 144,000.
A U.S. military base covers about one-third of the island, the westernmost U.S. territory, which is located 4,000 miles (6,440 km) west of Hawaii and 2,200 miles (3,540 km) southeast of Seoul.
